c.tagline: One of Islam's holiest cities, wrapped in a UNESCO-listed medina

taxi.fareNote: Metered taxis exist but drivers sometimes push for a flat negotiated fare with tourists; insist on the meter or agree a price beforehand

emergency.note: Response times can be slower than in coastal tourist areas; larger hotels can help coordinate assistance

avoid.reason: In the medina expect persistent carpet-shop touts and 'the museum is closed' style steering scams; keep valuables secure in crowded souks.

hood_desc: Kairouan's UNESCO-listed walled old city, home to the Great Mosque of Kairouan (Mosque of Uqba), one of the oldest and holiest mosques in the Islamic world. Maze-like souks sell the city's famous carpets and leather goods, and the whole quarter is ringed by 9th-century ramparts.

Named for the Zaouia of Sidi Sahbi, the ornately tiled 'Barber's Mosque' shrine to a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, this quarter draws pilgrims from across North Africa. It's quieter than the central medina but equally rich in Islamic architecture.

The area around the Bab Tunis gate on the medina's edge, a busy transition zone where traditional souks meet modern shops and transport hubs. It's a practical, workaday district good for local shopping and catching louages to other towns.

A modern strip on the edge of town built up with mid-range hotels catering to day-trippers visiting on tours from the coast. It lacks historic character but offers more comfort and easier parking than the medina.

The French colonial-era 'new town,' laid out with wider boulevards, the train station, and administrative buildings. It's more orderly and less atmospheric than the medina but useful for banks, pharmacies, and transport.

water.note: Officially treated but most visitors and many locals stick to bottled water.

transit.hours: Roughly 6am-8pm for local buses and louages; limited service after dark
transit.pay: Cash only, paid on board or at the louage station
transit.map: No official app; louage stations are organized by destination near the medina edge
transit.note: Most of the medina itself is only navigable on foot; louages are the practical way to reach other Tunisian cities

train: SNCFT regional rail connects Kairouan to Tunis and Sousse
bus: SNTRI intercity buses run from Tunis, Sousse, and other coastal cities

tip.r: Around 10% at sit-down restaurants is appreciated; small change for guides at the Great Mosque and taxi/louage drivers is customary

food.name: Makroudh
food.desc: Kairouan's emblem: diamonds of olive-oil semolina stuffed with date paste, fried and drenched in honey syrup, sold hot from the pan.

places.name: Makroudh Rqaya
places.note: Well-reviewed shop making trays fresh daily; the flavour locals send visitors for.

places.name: Makroudh Omrani
places.note: Another long-running maker on the sweet-shop run, boxes packed for travelling.

places.name: Souks around the Great Mosque
places.note: Rows of makroudh counters where you can watch the dough cut and fried.

food.name: Couscous bel osbane
food.desc: The regional feast couscous: steamed semolina in tomato broth with lamb and osbane, a herb-and-offal sausage stuffed by hand.

places.name: Restaurant Dar Abderrahman Zarrouk
places.note: Courtyard house serving a full spread of traditional Tunisian dishes including couscous.

places.name: Brothers Food
places.note: Praised for tagines and couscous cooked with fresh local ingredients.

places.name: Medina lunch canteens
places.note: Simple gargotes near Bab Tunis do a one-price couscous plate at midday only.

food.name: Lablabi
food.desc: Breakfast bowl of chickpeas in garlic-cumin broth poured over torn stale bread, crowned with an egg, harissa, olive oil and capers.

places.name: Medina lablabi counters
places.note: Tiny morning-only shops where you tear the bread into the bowl yourself.

places.name: Brothers Food
places.note: Sit-down version of the classic worker's breakfast, served with harissa on the side.

places.name: Avenue Habib Bourguiba eateries
places.note: Cheap everyday restaurants on the main avenue serving lablabi and ojja.

food.name: Kaak warka
food.desc: Delicate almond-paste rings perfumed with rose or geranium water under a pale sugar glaze, a Kairouan wedding and festival sweet.

places.name: Makroudh Rqaya
places.note: Sells kaak warka beside the makroudh, made fresh through the day.

places.name: Makroudh Omrani
places.note: Boxed rings of kaak warka sold as the standard gift from Kairouan.

places.name: Souks around the Great Mosque
places.note: Pastry stalls in the covered lanes stack them in glass cases by the tray.

food.name: Brik a l'oeuf
food.desc: Paper-thin malsouka pastry folded around egg, tuna, parsley and capers, deep fried and eaten fast before the yolk escapes.

places.name: Brothers Food
places.note: Standard starter here, fried to order so the yolk is still runny.

places.name: Restaurant Dar Abderrahman Zarrouk
places.note: Serves brik among its fried starters, including potato-roll versions.

places.name: Avenue Habib Bourguiba eateries
places.note: Every casual restaurant on the avenue fries brik at lunch for a dinar or two.

food.name: Ojja merguez
food.desc: Skillet of tomato, pepper and harissa with spicy merguez sausage and eggs cracked in at the end, mopped up with bread.

places.name: Avenue Habib Bourguiba eateries
places.note: The everyday hot-plate lunch on the main avenue, cooked in seconds.

places.name: Brothers Food
places.note: Reliable kitchen for ojja and grills if you want table service.

places.name: Medina lunch canteens
places.note: Small local canteens keep ojja going all afternoon alongside lablabi.

food.name: Mint tea with pine nuts
food.desc: Sweet green tea steeped with fresh mint and a spoon of toasted pine nuts floating on top; the social ritual of every Kairouan cafe.

places.name: Bir Barrouta cafe
places.note: Tea beside the famous well and its water wheel, a Kairouan landmark stop.

places.name: Medina cafes near Bab Tunis
places.note: Shaded terraces by the city gate where the glasses come loaded with pine nuts.

places.name: Avenue Habib Bourguiba cafes
places.note: Street-side tables for tea and people watching after the mosque visit.

food.name: Rouzata
food.desc: Milky almond cordial scented with orange-blossom water, served chilled; a non-alcoholic Tunisian celebration drink poured for guests.

places.name: Souks around the Great Mosque
places.note: Bottled almond and orange-blossom syrups sold beside the sweets and rose water.

places.name: Restaurant Dar Abderrahman Zarrouk
places.note: Traditional soft drinks and desserts served in the courtyard after a meal.

places.name: Bir Barrouta cafe
places.note: Cold almond drinks and citronnade for anyone tired of hot mint tea.

landmarks: Great Mosque of Kairouan (Mosque of Uqba)
Islam's fourth-holiest site and North Africa's oldest mosque, founded in 670 AD, its massive minaret and antique-columned prayer hall define early Islamic architecture.
Medina of Kairouan
A UNESCO-listed labyrinth of whitewashed lanes, blue doors, carpet workshops and makroudh pastry stalls enclosed within crenellated ochre ramparts.
Zaouia of Sidi Sahab (Mosque of the Barber)
A gorgeously tiled 17th-century shrine complex honoring Abu Zama'a, the Prophet's companion and barber, with courtyards of stucco lacework and Andalusian ceramics.
Aghlabid Basins
Vast 9th-century open-air reservoirs, marvels of medieval hydraulic engineering that once stored water channeled 36 kilometers from distant hills.
Mosque of the Three Doors (Mosquée des Trois Portes)
Built in 866 by an Andalusian scholar, its sculpted triple-arched facade of Kufic inscriptions and floral friezes is the world's oldest such decorated mosque front.
Bir Barrouta
A 17th-century covered well where a blindfolded camel turns the water wheel, its spring said to connect underground to Mecca's holy Zamzam.
Zaouia of Sidi Abid el Ghariani
A tranquil 14th-century mausoleum and former medersa with elegant courtyards, carved cedar ceilings and finely worked stucco deep in the medina.
City Walls and Gates (Bab Tunis and Bab ech Chouhada)
Kairouan's honey-colored brick ramparts, rebuilt over 11 centuries, funnel visitors through monumental gates into the medina's carpet souks.
Raqqada National Museum of Islamic Art
In a former presidential palace outside town, this museum showcases Aghlabid ceramics, rare blue-parchment Korans and treasures from Kairouan's golden age.
Kairouan Carpet Souks
The medina's storied carpet quarter, where knotted Kairouan rugs, famed across the Maghreb, are unfurled in cascades of crimson from vaulted showrooms.

train.note: Kairouan has no passenger rail service - the French-built narrow-gauge line from Sousse operated from 1882 until 1996 and no scheduled trains have run since. The nearest SNCFT stations are Sousse, about 60 km east, and Tunis, from where you finish the journey by coach or louage (https://www.sncft.com.tn/). For any Tunisian destination the bus or louage is faster than routing yourself via rail. No international trains are involved at any stage.

bus.note: The bus and louage stations sit together just outside the medina walls on the northwest side of town, a 15-20 minute walk or a very short taxi ride from the Great Mosque. SNTRI air-conditioned coaches reach Tunis in about 2.5-3 hours, with other services to Sousse, Sfax, Gafsa and Tozeur; tickets are bought at the counter shortly before departure. Shared louages leave when full and are the quickest way to Sousse, roughly an hour away. No scheduled international coach serves Kairouan - for Algeria or Libya you change in Tunis.

ferry.note: Kairouan sits about 60 km inland on the central Tunisian plain with no port or navigable water, so no ferry service exists; the nearest scheduled sailings are the Sfax-Kerkennah Islands ferry and the international CTN ships from La Goulette in Tunis.

half.name: El Jem
half.blurb: A Roman amphitheater built around 238 AD once held 35,000 spectators and remains one of the best-preserved coliseums outside Italy.

half.name: Sousse
half.blurb: A walled Mediterranean medina with a 9th-century ribat fortress and Great Mosque sits on the coast east of Kairouan.

half.name: Monastir
half.blurb: A coastal ribat fortress, the Bourguiba family mausoleum, and an old harbor make up this seaside town's historic center.

full.name: Sbeitla
full.blurb: Roman ruins including three adjoining temples, a forum, and a triumphal arch remain from the ancient city of Sufetula.
